utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, would I like to remind you that the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony still binds you. Ms. De Landri, are you ready to continue your cross-examination? MS. DE LANDRI: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed. MS. DE LANDRI: Thank you. Cross-examination by Ms. De Landri: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, I'd like to direct your attention to the events of August 1995 again. MS. DE LANDRI: And if we could have the witness's statement, D1723, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cipci, were you in Knin on August 6, 1995, when General Cermak arrived?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have anything on the screen but the first page of my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, could you answer the question. If Ms. De Landri will take you to a specific portion that will then appear on your screen, but the first question was whether you were in Knin on August 6, 1995, when General Cermak arrived. Were you or were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was. MS. DE LANDRI:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you speak with the general at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What -- to the best you can recall, what did you do on August 6th of 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 6th of August, the president was also supposed to arrive. Franjo Tudjman was supposed to arrive. And he was also supposed to go from Knin to Kijevo. That's why I'd been asked by my minister to put everything in place for the president's security as he was driving from Knin to Kijevo. Since I was in Knin already on the 5th and the Kijevo-Knin road seemed to me very dangerous due to a large number of military trucks carrying ammunition, I telephoned the president's office and asked them to give up on that plan and that the president didn't go to Kijevo because this road seemed too dangerous to me. Despite all that, I took a team of police officers and traffic policemen on motorbikes and I arrived in Knin on the 6th to meet the president, and if need be, I was ready to transport him to Kijevo, and that's why I was in Knin already in the morning of the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But can you be a little bit more specific about what exactly you did on that day.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day I arrived in the morning, and I was in the place where the president was supposed to land by his helicopter at the football pitch in Knin. That's where I parked all the vehicles that we brought, all the cars and motorbikes, and I ordered my officers to find themselves a place to sit and wait for the outcome of the developments. And when Mr. Franjo Tudjman arrived and landed, I was with the group of people who met him in front of the helicopter. After the landing I went -- he went to the fortress and I remained in the football pitch with my men, and I waited for the president to return. And when the president returned, I was told that the president wouldn't go to Kijevo, but, rather, that he would take a helicopter and fly to Drnis. After that, I gathered my men and we headed for Split. I would like to say something else. On the 6th in the morning, my minister was also in Knin, Ivan Jarnjak was also there, and I spoke to him with regard to General Cermak as well. I heard that General Cermak had arrived in Knin and that he had certain duties, that he had been given certain tasks, and then I asked my minister Mr. Jarnjak as to what Mr. Cermak --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you for one second. I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- I just would like to direct you now to your statement, to paragraph 17 of your statement. Do you have that in front of you now? Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just directing your attention to the 14th line of the statement where it's written: "I asked what his function was," referring to General Cermak. Who did you ask what his function was?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just told you I asked my minister, Mr. Ivan Jarnjak. He was there on the 6th as well. He was in Knin on the 6th in the morning, and he was the one who told me, who answered. And I also, in my subsequent conversations with the minister, either with the minister he, himself, or one of his assistants or his deputy, I was provided the same information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But tell us precisely what the information was.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information was that Mr. Cermak had been sent to Knin by Mr. Franjo Tudjman. Mr. Franjo Tudjman reactivated him from the reserve force and promoted him to an active army general and that he was sent because Mr. Cermak was a high-quality economist before that, with an intention for him to try and put everything in place for the normalisation of the situation in Knin, in the Knin region, and if possible, for the economy to be revived there. And this is more or less what they told me in my subsequent conversations with ministry officials. Even the assistant minister who arrived in Knin shortly after Storm. Mrs. Katica Osrecki told me that. I believe she had known Mr. Cermak from before. I was her escort through Knin. We came to pay a visit to Mr. Cermak together, and in a conversation going to his office that's what she told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Directing your attention again to that conversation that you just spoke about that you had with Minister Jarnjak. Who else was present, if any one, during that conversation?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that my chief of the police sector was also there. He was with me, and he was in charge and responsible to organise everything that was necessary in case President Tudjman wanted to travel from Knin to Kijevo as had been announced. And when our minister arrived, there was also Mr. Josko Moric. I don't know whether he was present during that particular conversation. Of course the minister greeted all of us from the police because we all knew each other very well, and I'm sure that Mr. Jure Radalj, who was permanently by my side, he was also present when I spoke to Mr. Jarnjak and when I asked him that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm also going to direct your attention now to paragraph 18 in your statement, and specifically to line 25 where you've said that: "Mr. Cermak had no military authority over them," meaning troops, military command in the army situated in the building next to where his office was. MS. DE LANDRI: And I'd ask if we could have another document, D31.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, I'd ask you to look at that document. It's not necessary for you to read it aloud. Just take a moment to look at it, and I'm going to ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead. I've read the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I think we can agree that it's a letter of appointment by the president appointing General Cermak the garrison commander of the Knin Garrison; is that right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can see. That's what I can read in the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's dated August 5, 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. De Landri, is it really necessary to ask that? I mean, if the witness would say no, it's the 12th," I think this document we've seen this now 10 if not 15 times. Is it really -- try to get to the core of what you want to ask this witness. And I could tell you that the task of a garrison commander under the law, the position of a garrison commander, in view of combat operations, military combat operations, the understanding or misunderstanding of some 30, 40, or 50 people about whether they knew exactly what it was or not, whether they knew the legislation or not, the documents issued by Mr. Cermak and whether these were orders or were non-orders, we've gone through that some 15 or 20 times. If this witness, you think, could add substantially something to this, if you have any reason to believe that, then ask focused questions on those matters, and let's not ask the witness whether this really is a document dated the 5th of August, because we've gone through that, I think, 20 or 25 times. And unless you have any reason to believe that this witness has information which makes this document not authentic or that it would have been issued on another date, of course you're perfectly free to ask whatever questions. If, however, there's no reason whatsoever to believe that, then to ask him whether this is an appointment letter for Mr. Cermak, whether it is dated the 5th of October, whether it is signed by Dr. Tudjman, that's all, I would say, not in dispute, and I'd like you to move forward in such a way that the Chamber gets information in addition to the huge pile of information we have already on this matter. Please proceed. MS. DE LANDRI: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, did you have any conversations with President Tudjman about Mr. Cermak's authority?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had several conversations with President Tudjman. The first time in 1960 when he became president. I had several conversations with him, but Mr. Cermak's name never came up in any of those conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. My question was: Did you ever have any conversations with him about Mr. Cermak's authority, and in particular, his appointment pursuant to this document this, letter?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've already answered no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what is your basis for your statement in paragraph 18 that Mr. Cermak had no military authority over those troops?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to explain that yesterday. The basis for that is the fact that as I was assuming duties as the chief of the police administration of Split and Dalmatia, I was duty-bound to study all the laws, including military laws in Split, which is a much bigger city with a lot more combat units, including also the command of the navy. I had a garrison commander, Mr. Zoricic. During the four years of war while I was the chief of the police administration there -- you asked me what was my basis for my claim, and I'm trying to answer that. Throughout the four years of war I never had a single official meeting with the garrison commander of Split, and at the same time, I had official meetings with every other commander, including Admiral Letica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't have any specific information about Mr. Cermak's situation. Is that accurate? Just focus your answer on the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- I mean, Mr. Cermak's situation, he was asked the question about what he knew about Mr. Cermak's appointment. He gave that conversation with Minister Jarnjak. I hope it's not seen that I'm being obstructive here, but the witness, I could detect, was getting frustrated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I understood your last answer, Mr. Cipci, to be that your statement in paragraph 18 that Mr. Cermak had no military authority over those troops was based on your understanding of legal provisions in relation to command structures and the position of a garrison commander. That took us a while to get to that, but now, Ms. De Landri, do you -- do you seek to further explore the formal position or the practical position, and if you would please then put the questions in such a way that the witness has no difficulties in -- both in understanding the question and also does not have an impression that it's a matter that we have dealt with already. Please proceed. MS. DE LANDRI: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps -- perhaps I could ask one question which I think you may have on your mind. You based your answer on your understanding of the legal provision. Are you aware of any element in the position of Mr. Cermak which is not either supported by or consistent with what we find in the legal instruments about the position of a garrison commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if Mr. Cermak received from anybody authorities that were beyond the law or above the law. I believe that even Mr. Franjo Tudjman would have indicated that in the decision, at least in the footnotes. He would have added that, and he would have worded it perhaps that Mr. Cermak, in addition to the authorities given to him as the garrison commander, he has some other authorities as well. I really don't know who was it who could have given Mr. Cermak any higher authorities if not the supreme commander of the armed forces who was also the one who actually issued the decision in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your answer, more or less, is no, you're not aware of anything beyond what is in the formal position of a garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, the witness did mention his factual experience --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- at particularly from the garrison commander Mr. Zoricic, and was dealing with those issues from his experience, and his statement also deals with his experience in relation to that matter. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since -- since the matter is raised by Ms. De Landri, I would just like to try to get focused answers, and the witness apparently says that no additional authority had been given to him on paper. Therefore, there was no additional authority. Whether that's the whole picture or not, that's another matter, but that's the answer of the witness at this moment. Please proceed, Ms. De Landri. MS. DE LANDRI: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, I'd like to direct your attention to paragraph 22 of your statement. Oh. That's Exhibit P1723. Now, in paragraph 22 you'd stated, and there was some testimony to this effect yesterday, that you were the only official in Knin who could authorise civilians to pass through that district. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is not accurate, so the answer can't be either. I was not the only official in Knin. I was the only authorised person to issue passes for people to cross the check-points that were under the control of my police administration, and I'm talking about the area above Vrlika, Sinj, Vrlika, and border crossings, and for the passage through those border crossings I was the one who was authorised to issue passes which allowed people entry into the liberated area. Thus I was not the only authorised person in Knin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we agree that you had the authority to issue the passes, and you -- that that authority derived from your position as a civilian police authority. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That authority was based on the order issued by the Minister of the Interior, Mr. Ivan Jarnjak, as well as based on the fact that I was the chief of the police administration. Therefore, at meetings that we held before Operation Storm, it was expressly said that the chiefs of police administrations would be issuing passes for people to pass through their border check-points. My border check-points were beyond the town of Vrlika. Do you need further clarification? I can tell you that the -- that you could also enter the liberated area of Krajina from Sibenik, Zadar, and other areas, and the respective chiefs of police administrations were in charge of the border crossings in those areas, and I'm talking about Zadar, Sibenik, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we've looked at some documents yesterday, and I'm going to direct your attention to them in a moment, in which you wrote some letters to the Ministry of the Interior asking for clarification about some passes. MS. DE LANDRI: And I believe those are D494 and 495. If we could have those. 494 first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement you said: "Mr. Cermak was not authorised to issue passes to civilians." Do you recall that? And I'd like to direct --

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention now to this exhibit. It's D494. Have you had a moment to look at that document?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document that I signed, and I sent it to my ministry. Is that the document that I'm looking at?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is -- it was written on the 15th of August. I can see my signature, and there's also a footnote in my own handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you, Mr. Cipci, is if Mr. Cermak did not have the authority to issue passes to civilians, why did you not write that at the time when you wrote this letter or memo to the Interior Ministry on August 15th of 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I wrote this -- if you look at the last sentence, you will see that it reads: "Please reply and confirm in writing the validity of the passes." The word "validity" means whether they were valid or not, because they were not in compliance with what had been agreed, and I asked from the ministry to confirm whether the passes were valid on the assumption that something had been changed in the meantime. The reply I received was that Mr. Cermak could no longer issue passes for civilians but only for military personnel and for civilians serving in the Croatian Army. That was the answer that I received from the ministry, and I believe that Mr. Cermak later on indicated on his passes that his passes were valid only for military personnel and civilians serving in the Croatian Army. Therefore, you can see that this was my written request for an explanation from the ministry as to whether Cermak's passes were valid or not. I thought that they were not valid. And as for Mr. Cermak, when he showed me a pass of that kind in his office I told him, "Mr. Cermak, all civilians that I find in my territory carrying your pass I'm going to remove from my area," and that did occur.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure there's an answer to the question. You stated unequivocally in your written statement that you submitted to the Court that there -- there was -- you were -- you were the only individual who had that authority, but that's not expressed in the document that was written at the time back in August of 1995. Is there a reason why it wasn't expressed then but it's expressed some 14 years later?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't understand what you're aiming at, what you're asking me. I have just told you that I was the only person authorised to let people go through my check-points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. De Landri is asking you the following: In this letter which you have explained to us to be an instrument to verify the accuracy of your own opinion that Mr. Cermak was not entitled to issue passes, why at the time you didn't write to the Ministry, "I sent you this pass. It's my view that General Cermak steps beyond his authority by issuing those passes instead of seeking confirmation of the validity." That's what you'd like to know. MS. DE LANDRI: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect and -- I don't see a big difference here. I don't see any major difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand your answer correctly if I think that you are saying that you raised the issue but not in the sharp way as Ms. De Landri would have expected you to do in view of your statement that Mr. Cermak was not authorised issue those passes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I may have not been stern enough in the written document, but I was very strict when I removed from that territory people whom I found there with Mr. Cermak's passes, and that was before, even before I sent my query to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. De Landri. MS. DE LANDRI: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, I believe yesterday you testified that your visits to Knin were in a "semi-private capacity"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm wondering if you can explain to the Trial Chamber how if you were in that location in a semi-private capacity you had the authority to issue the passage of civilians in that area.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, madam. I obviously can't understand your questions. I am repeating for the fifth time: I was the authorised person for the area of my responsibility, which was the police administration of Split and Dalmatia. It was my police administration, the police administration of Split and Dalmatia from which you could enter the liberated area of Knin, and I had several check-points for which I issued passes. I did not issue passes in Knin. I'm repeating this for the fifth time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to continue and direct your attention to paragraph 25 of your statement. MS. DE LANDRI: Can we have Exhibit D1723. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's paragraph 23. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see the first part of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're -- you may recall from memory without having to look at the document that you stated that you confronted Mr. Cermak about the passes, and you asked him about his issuance of those passes. Can you tell the Trial Chamber when that conversation occurred?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, first of all, you have to bear in mind that that happened over 15 years ago, so I don't know when exactly that conversation took place, but I know that it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, you do not have to tell Ms. De Landri what she has to keep on her mind. If you do not know any more after 15 years, fine, tell us, but please try to answer the questions and focus on what is asked. The question was: When did the conversation occur? If you know, tell us. If you know it not on a precise date but, rather, say, within a range after couple of days, tell us as well. If you don't know any more, tell us also. Please proceed with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That conversation took place certainly a few days after Operation Storm, but I don't know exactly when that was. MS. DE LANDRI:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. As best you can recall, can you tell us what was -- who was present first?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Cermak and myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did the conversation take place?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In his office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what did you say to him?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Good morning, Mr. Cermak. Here I am. I came to have a cup of coffee with you and have a little chat."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, you certainly have understood that Ms. De Landri asked you what you said to Mr. Cermak in relation to the passes. So if you'd please be kind enough to tell us what you told General Cermak in relation to the validity of the passes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] In an informal conversation that we had, because my visit was not official, Mr. Cermak took out a pile of passes that he had printed, and then I told him that those passes were not in compliance with what my minister had told me, and that was that the passes could be issued only by the chiefs of police administrations for the passage through their respective check-points, and that for that reason, until I was told differently by my minister, I would not be inclined to let the civilians through to the liberated area if they carried his passes. They would be allowed to do so only with the passes issued by myself, and that is my answer to the question put to me. MS. DE LANDRI:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did General Cermak have any comments to you, Mr. Cipci?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how long did your meeting last?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not more than half an hour. That's how long it took me to have a cup of coffee, smoke my pipe, and had a chat. I had arrived in Knin for different reasons, but it seemed a decent thing to do to pay a visit to Mr. Cermak. I also always paid a visit to Mr. Pasic, who was the mayor of Knin of sorts, the commissioner of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you start telling us all other persons you paid a visit to, you've answered the question. That was half an hour, that meeting. Please proceed. MS. DE LANDRI:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, I'd like to direct your to paragraph 21 in your statement. Now, if I understood your answers to the last series of questions correctly, you said the meeting that you had with General Cermak about the passes occurred in his office. Here in paragraph 21, in the first sentence, you say: "I was never present at meetings which were held in General Cermak's office." Which is correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we have the full context, please? The witness stressed informally at the start of his testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- and also in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. De Landri, the question as put to the witness, which of the two is correct, is unfair if we do not include the remainder, the other sentences of paragraph 21. MS. DE LANDRI: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we -- I'll refrain from further comment. Please proceed. MS. DE LANDRI:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you take a moment to look at paragraph 21, Mr. Cipci.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer? Both are correct. I did go to Cermak's office, but I never attended an official meeting. In other words, both are correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The meeting that you referred to involving the passes, that was not an official meeting, in your view?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way. I just came to say hello, and then in that informal conversation he showed me that pile of passes. That's what I told you. I did not have any reason to pay Cermak an official visit, because Knin was not within the area of my official responsibility. My area of responsibility ended with Vrlika.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just another question. You had in paragraph -- I believe it's paragraph 23 also of your statement, you said you would expel anyone who came into the jurisdiction with passes issued by General Cermak. Did that ever, in fact, occur? Did you expel anyone who came into the jurisdiction with a pass issued by the general?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My officers informed me that some foreigners could be found in the area of my responsibility carrying General Cermak's passes. They told me they didn't know what to do. I instructed them to escort them through the border pass and escort them from the area of our responsibility and send them towards Knin, and that's what happened. MS. DE LANDRI: Could we have P509 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Cipci, I'll ask you to take a look at that document for a moment.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Have you seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think we can agree that that's - excuse me - an order dated August 15th, 1995, signed by Colonel-General Cermak, allowing the movement of civilians to the town of Knin without passes. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you -- you say you've not seen that before testifying today in this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. MS. DE LANDRI: I'd ask for P510, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to take a look at that document, Mr. Cipci, and read that document, and first ask you if you've seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The document's under seal, Your Honour, I'm reminded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar has taken care of the matter. Please proceed. MS. DE LANDRI: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to take a look at that document?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen it before today?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted) During the four years in office, I must have seen hundreds of documents every day. So we're talking about thousands during the term of office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that one of the main themes of your written statement to the Court is, first, that General Cermak did not have the authority to issue the passes. My first question to you is if he did not have the authority to issue the passes, as we've seen in the first document that you've been shown, why was there an order that he issued saying that the passes were no longer necessary? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe. One second, please. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just -- could we just go into private session very briefly, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. MS. DE LANDRI:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second page of the document under paragraph C, I'd ask you to have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I have it in Croatian, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it's -- there should be a paragraph C in Croatian. It should be on the right-hand side of your screen. Have you had a moment to read that?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you is can you explain how General Cermak was able to arrange for the freedom of movement of the ECMM monitors without your intervention on August 18th?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what area was this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I believe it says on the front of the document. If you'd turn your attention to the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I got the impression that it was in Dabar, as it reads, with the grid coordinates. At least that's the event described as -- MS. DE LANDRI:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's in the upper left-hand corner, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. De Landri, we are talking about what is written there under C. That's an event where Mr. Cermak was called. That's what you are referring to? MS. DE LANDRI: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, it seems to me that there is an indication in that same paragraph of the place where this took place, would you agree with that, and that apparently is what the witness would like to know in order to answer your question, whether he has an explanation for that. Now you take him back to the first page, but would it not be more logical to tell him that what happened here happened, at least as far as I'm aware, I do not know exactly where to locate it, in Dabar? XJ2554. MS. DE LANDRI: No, the question is for him to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The witness says, Where did this happen. And then you say, Look at page 1. Whereas in the paragraph I see what seems to be, at least that's how I understand it, to be a geographical location, that is the combined Croatian MUP military police check-point in Dabar. So there exactly they were stopped. There -- at least that's how I understand it. That's where that phone call was made. And the witness asked where was it. Would you agree with me that because it's important for him, you're asking for an explanation, it's apparently important for the witness to know where it happened. So should we then not inform the witness that it looks on this document that it happened in Dabar rather than -- I do not know what I could find better on page 1 than I find in this very paragraph which describes where it happened, unless my understanding of the document is incorrect. Okay. Apparently the stopping the monitors took place in Dabar. If that is relevant for your answer, then please be informed about that, and then could you please explain as Ms. De Landri asked you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If it took place in Dabar and if the question is how could Mr. Cermak have dealt with the issue without me, then my answer is that Dabar was not in my area of responsibility. Mr. Cermak had absolutely no reason to contact me, and he did not. The same applies to those manning the check-point. They did not need to get in touch with my chief but, rather, with the chief who was superior to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, next question. You say Dabar is not within your area of responsibility. Is that -- now, could you explain whether Mr. Cermak could deal with the matter directly to the extent the persons involved could observe?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on this paragraph, it turns out that Mr. Cermak indeed took part in it and resolved the problem. That is a fact, but that's also all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say, "I have no explanation as to what his authority or role could have been here." Please proceed, Ms. De Landri. MS. DE LANDRI: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we get P957, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my information, Dabar is approximately where, because I wouldn't know. No one knows. Could you tell us where approximately Dabar is? MS. DE LANDRI: I'm being told, excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But -- MS. DE LANDRI: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I'd like to hear it from the witness. Could you tell us where it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly. I think it's to the west from Krajina. It wasn't in the area bordering on the Split-Dalmatia county, at least I think; although, I must say I'm not certain. These are small border check-points and hamlets of which there are thousands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So not knowing exactly where it is, it may have been difficult for you to establish that it was not in your area of responsibility, isn't it, if you can't tell us where it is? You cannot for sure tell us that it was outside your area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm positive it was not in my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although you do not know where it is. Please proceed, Ms. De Landri. MS. DE LANDRI: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have P957 in front of you? I'd like to direct your attention to paragraph 2. Have you had an opportunity to read paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I'm just directing your attention to the first part of it. In particular, I want to ask you about the sentence that reads: "Today we went to General Cermak to complain about our ROM restriction of movement yesterday in Vrlika area. He apologised to us for this accident that will never happen again. Military and civilian police should know that all IOs have Fom in the area. He was for sure that one of the low-ranking officers was acting by self-initiative. The General reacted immediately by phoning the minister of internal affairs and asking him to contact -- to contact with the civil police in Split to establish coordination to avoid those accidents in the future. He told us that the officer will be punish. TC: The angry way of phoning the minister gave us the idea that he really wants to have good relationship with the ECMM. EC." My question to you, Mr. Cipci, is does that change your view at all about Mr. Cermak's relationship with the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It absolutely does not. The stress should be placed on the word "he asked," Minister Jarnjak. If you can order someone something, you don't need to ask. MS. DE LANDRI: Mr. President, this might and good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It may be, but before we have the break, Mr. Cipci, I'm just trying to find out exactly the boundaries of your area of responsibility going in south-easterly direction from Vrlika. Then you go in the direction of Sinj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's Sinj, Vrlika, Knin, or the other way round.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I am right in understanding that Sinj is south-east of Vrlika.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, to the south-east. Vrlika is somewhat higher up on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in easterly direction of Vrlika, where did your responsibility end.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the west of Vrlika, towards Kijevo. Sinj, Vrlika, and then Kijevo. The boundary was between Vrlika and Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I wasn't asking you in a westerly direction, but from the town of Vrlika to the east, how far did your area of responsibility extend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sinj was also within my area of responsibility. It is within the boundaries of what today is the Split-Dalmatia county. That was the border of my area of responsibility and the territory of the Split-Dalmatia police administration. The borders of the Split-Dalmatia county are also the borders of the Split-Dalmatia police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, by way of assistance to the Chamber, there was a series of maps that we put in, D806, if that would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll have a -- D806, you said. Just let me have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was a sequence of maps that we admitted some time ago, and it was a series of three maps. I think the pertinent map is map 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll have a look at it, because I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And then map 3 as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just checking the maps, Mr. Cipci. I'm afraid that these maps do not fully help me out. Could I ask you again. Going from Vrlika, going in south-easterly direction, that is direction of Hrvace and Sinj. Yes? Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am. One goes towards Sinj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would that whole area be within your area of responsibility, from Vrlika to Sinj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in easterly direction, would that -- would your area of responsibility go up to the border to Bosnia. And when I say easterly direction, I'm moving to the right, but you would --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the east and south-east of Sinj, there is the border with Bosnia and the area ends with the Bosnian border. All the way to the east from my area of responsibility there is Bosnia again. So we have the border with Bosnia, the border towards Sibenik, and Vrlika, which at the time was the Zadar-Knin administration and now it is Sibenik-Knin administration. This is where the borders were: Bosnia on one side, Sibenik on the other side, the sea on the third side. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, between Vrlika and Sinj there seems to be a lake. I take it that it's an electrical plant which created that lake. Is that a rather long lake. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is an artificial lake which was made because of the hydroelectric plant of Peruca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, was that lake entirely within your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is difficult for me to say where the border was exactly once you go beyond Knin -- Sinj. In any case, Vrlika was, and everything to the west of Vrlika, that was still within.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The lake, at least, I take it from maps I'm consulting at this very moment, is somewhere between Vrlika and Sinj. Not south of Sinj but north-west of Sinj. Was that artificial lake entirely in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say. I am not certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you can tell us what was within your area of responsibility and what not, then I at least expect you to be able to know where your area of responsibility was, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is, but you need to know that my area of responsibility in terms of size was the greatest one in Croatia, and it still is. It is still the largest police administration and the greatest one in terms of number of staff. I didn't tour each and every village. I had under me the city of Split with 200.000 inhabitants and 12 other towns. This is what I visited. I didn't go into each and every municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It now appears that you do not know where the borders are of your area of responsibility, and it also appears that you do not know where Dabar is, and nevertheless you come with a strong statement that it was not in your area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I claim that as far as I can recall at this point in time, Dabar was not within my AOR. I do not recall having Dabar as a crossing. In -- maybe I'm wrong, but at this point in time I think Dabar was not within my AOR. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course we expect you to tell us what you know for certain. For the parties' information, if I look at Google maps, I see a Dabar in Croatia, approximately 1 mile east from this lake, between Vrlika and Sinj. And if the parties could assist Chamber in establishing where in August 1995 the exact borders of the area of responsibility of this witness were that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One thing, Mr. President, that may assist, and I'd have to go back to a different map, often times in this area we have villages of same name and the key point here, I think, is this grid reference, this NATO grid reference of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that would help --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as I said before, I'm -- and I think I was quite transparent, the maps I'm consulting at this moment because on the maps you've shown, you drew our attention to, I do not know whether we have the exact borders, at least not described in the way as the witness says was his area of responsibility. That's the reason, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But every assistance by the parties to find out whether this Dabar is the Dabar we're talking about and whether this Dabar would be within or outside the zone of responsibility would assist the Chamber in further assessing the reliability and credibility of the answer that was an explanation on how Mr. Cermak could deal with the matter without the intervention of the witness. We will have a break, and we'll continue at five minutes past 11.00. One -- Ms. De Landri, your time limit of yesterday, do you still think you could keep it to two -- two sessions? MS. DE LANDRI: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you are not only encouraged but even instructed to do it, because that's the time the Chamber, having assessed the efficiency of the cross-examination, allows you to continue. We will resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. De Landri, please proceed. MS. DE LANDRI: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, you said in your statement, your written statement, that Mr. Cermak did not command the civil police. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber why it is, in that case, that he would have received reports of ordinary criminal activity during the relevant time period?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who and why sent such reports to Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, maybe it would be -- assist you if I showed you some of those reports. MS. DE LANDRI: Could we show the witness 65 ter 2806.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to summarise briefly, I think if you have a moment to look at the document I think we can agree that that's a report from Chief Cetina to General Cermak about several murders?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Excuse me. I don't see the word "report." I see "We hereby advise you that we have completed the necessary checks."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A written communication in relation to, would that do, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm concerned about terminology that's used and I hope the Bench can sometimes appreciate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's why I suggested --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a more neutral way, and -- MS. DE LANDRI: No objection to that terminology, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection, so that's then accepted. Please proceed. MS. DE LANDRI:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just ask the witness if he can explain why, in view of his statement in his report, General Cermak might have received this advice from Chief Cetina.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, the chief of the Zadar Police Administration, as I can see sent this document to the Knin Garrison command for General Cermak's attention, but this means that the official report had been sent to someone else, probably to his superior, that is to say the ministry in Zagreb, and only for attention to General Cermak. It was General Cermak's duty to establish quality co-operation with both the civilian police and the governmental commissioner so as to be able to do his work. Therefore, Cetina did not send the report to Cermak. He simply informed him. He brought to his attention the fact that there was a report he had submitted to his superior. I believe this falls within the framework of quality co-operation. MS. DE LANDRI: Your Honour, I'd like to tender this document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2649.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2649 is admitted into evidence. MS. DE LANDRI: Could we have D487 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. De Landri, I'm informed that this is a document which should not be shown to the public. MS. DE LANDRI: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please be very precise in that. MS. DE LANDRI: Yes, Your Honour. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you also, when you put questions to the witness, consider whether we have to go into private session for those questions or whether we can deal with the matter in public. MS. DE LANDRI: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps in view of what we did earlier, it would be wiser to go into private session. MS. DE LANDRI: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. De Landri. MS. DE LANDRI: Yes. I just wanted to direct the witness's attention to 65 ter 3289.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have that document in front of you, Mr. Cipci?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you see that that's dated October 11th, 1995, and in the B/C/S version, on the lower right-hand side, is that Chief Cetina's signature?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but the name that is typed does say "Ivica Cetina," although I don't know whether this is his signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is again, this document appears to report ordinary criminal activity, and it's from Mr. Cetina to General Cermak. Do you know why Chief Cetina would be making this report to General Cermak in October of 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose for the same reasons I specified before. As of day one, General Cermak was requested information by various international monitors, and they also submitted their complaints to him. It is quite certain that General Cermak wanted to be informed about the incidents taking place in the area so as to be able to provide quality and relevant information to the international monitors and international organisation if they asked for any information. In the document we saw before, one could notice that he had no information about the murder and the rape, and hence he sought that information from Mr. Romanic. It probably became a practice that co-operation be established between Cermak and the civilian police in a way that they would report to him such events so that he would be informed should anyone from the international institutions require information on those. I don't know what the exact case was, and I don't know why Cetina sent it. I can only see it before me. And based on my previous experience working for the police, that is the context in which I see this document. MS. DE LANDRI: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P2650.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2650 is admitted into evidence. You may proceed. MS. DE LANDRI: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, are you aware that there is evidence in this case that Mr. Cermak had daily meetings with representatives of the civilian and military police in Knin?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he did have meetings. I heard that during my stays in Knin. I heard it from Mr. Pasic, whom I knew. I heard that he held regular meetings with Mr. Cermak, that the chief of police was also present, as well as the representatives of some other institutions such as the Red Cross and others. All those who were duty-bound to deal with the situation in Knin were supposed to have regular briefings in order to coordinate their activities. Mr. Pasic had whole quality co-operation with the civilian police and others, and the same applied to Mr. Cermak. He had to co-operate well with the representative of the government of the Republic of Croatia as well as the civilian police. Those were the factors that were to be on the same page and -- and they were supposed to deal with the situation in the liberated area. It is not surprising that they met every day, because there were daily problems starting with water, electricity, cleanliness, food supply, and each of them had an area that they had to focus on and deal with. That mutual assistance between the representative of the government, Mr. Cermak, the civilian protection, the Red Cross, the police, had to function if they wanted to do their job well and if they wanted to accomplish the mission for which they had been sent to the liberated area. Mr. President, can I say another sentence, please? It would be much more logical to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I will allow you to add one sentence, but from the whole of your answer I understood that your answer to the previous question was that you were aware that these meetings took place. May I invite you to see what Ms. De Landri specifically wants to know, and here she only asked for your awareness of this evidence. If you'd like to add one sentence, I'll allow you to do that but keep it to one sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did know, and it would have been more logical if the meetings had been held in Mr. Pasic's office, because he was the representative of the Croatian government. But Pasic told me that his office was not conducive to such meetings. He did not have conditions conducive to holding such meetings in his office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we further discuss the logic of where the meetings took place, let's try to find out what Ms. De Landri would like to elicit from you. Ms. De Landri. MS. DE LANDRI:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Cipci, that in 1998, Mr. Cermak himself said that he had meetings and talks with Minister Jarnjak about matters having to do with the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find it only normal that Mr. Cermak had contacts with Minister Jarnjak. It was also logical to me when Mr. Cermak started receiving complaints from the monitors on day two or three after Operation Storm, that he sent a letter to the prime minister, to the president of the state who appointed him, the minister of defence, and the minister of the interior, to inform them about the events that he had learnt about from the international monitors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I hope, as a matter of fact, that the parties could agree on that, and then the next question is where are exactly the boundaries of the area of responsibility of this witness. I meanwhile would like to use my time, and Mr. Cipci will forgive me, to read the reasons, the Chamber's reasons for its decision of the 31st of August, 2009, denying the Prosecution's objection to documents to be used with expert witness Anthony R. Jones. On the 27th of August, 2009, the Prosecution filed its objection to documents to be used with expert witness Jones. It submitted that out of 37 documents which the Gotovina Defence indicated it may use with the witness, 14 were not referred to in his expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Secondly, the Prosecution requested the Chamber to preclude the Gotovina Defence from presenting 7 of the 14 documents to the witness during his testimony if those documents had not been provided to him at the time he drafted his report. The Prosecution added that these seven documents were key exhibits pertaining to central issues in the case. Finally, the Prosecution requested the Chamber to preclude the Gotovina Defence from presenting two of the 14 documents to the witness because they concerned the manner in which Serb civilians left Krajina which, according to the Prosecution, is an issue that is outside of the scope of the witness's expert report and unrelated to his expertise. The Prosecution argued that allowing the Gotovina Defence to use the nine documents it objected to, would be tantamount to eliciting an oral addendum to the expert report without adequate notice to the Prosecution. In its response of the 28th of August, 2009, the Gotovina Defence submitted it was not required to provide notice whether the 14 documents were provided to the witness prior to the drafting of his report. It argued that the general disclosure obligations of the Defence were governed by Rule 67(A) and that it had satisfied its disclosure obligations under Rule 94 bis. In relation to the seven documents objected to, the Gotovina Defence submitted the Prosecution had been allowed to use documents which were not referred to in the expert report of witness Konings during his testimony in the Prosecution's case. It added that the Prosecution could remedy its concerns by cross-examining the witness. As the two documents objected to, the Gotovina Defence argued that it had given notice of the evidence it intended to present through proper disclosure and that the documents are within expert witness Jones's knowledge and are relevant and probative to his expert report. Lastly, the Gotovina Defence argued that the Prosecution's objection was premature as the proper time to object would be during the witness's testimony or when the witness's written evidence was being tendered. On the 31st of August, 2009, in an oral decision with reasons to follow, the Chamber denied the Prosecution's objection. This can be found at transcript pages 20890 through 20891. In its written decision on disclosure of expert materials of the 27th of August, 2009, the Chamber held that there's no obligation for the Defence to disclose to the Prosecution lists of all the information provided to their proposed expert witnesses. The Chamber's oral decision to deny the Prosecution's request for a notification of which, if any, of the 14 documents were provided to the witness prior to the drafting of his expert report, was in line with this written decision and rendered for the same reasons. With regard to the request to preclude the Gotovina Defence from using the nine documents objected to with the witness, the Chamber recalled that it had -- it has previously held in paragraph 7 of its decision on part of the Gotovina Defence's Rule 73 motion in limine of the 21st of May, 2008, that if proper notice has been given, a party may examine an expert witness with respect to matters not included in his expert report, so long as they are relevant, probative, and within the witness's expertise. In relation to the seven documents, the Prosecution did not dispute that these documents were relevant, probative, and within the witness's expertise. The Chamber saw no reason to preclude the Defence from using these documents with the witness and found that the Prosecution's concerns could be addressed during cross-examination. In relation to the two documents, which according to the Prosecution fall outside the scope of the witness's expertise, the Chamber considered that the two documents do not only address the manner in which Serbs left Krajina, but also issues of a military nature such as the regrouping of the RSK Army and the military situation in Krajina on the 4th of August, 1995. The Chamber found these issues relevant, probative, and within the witness's expertise and that the Defence should not be precluded from using the documents with the witness. With regard to adequate notice that certain documents would be used with the witness, the Chamber considered that, in e-mails of the 18th and the 20th of August, 2009, the Gotovina Defence had notified the Prosecution and the Chamber that it may use the 14 documents with Jones. This was well in advance of Jones's first day of testimony on the 31st of August, 2009. Further, the nine documents had already been admitted into evidence prior to August 2009, and the Prosecution was well aware of their contents. And for these reasons, the Chamber denied the Prosecution's objection, and this concludes the reasons for the Chamber's decision on this matter. Mr. Cipci, we abused the opportunity of your absence -- we abused the opportunity of your absence to read a decision. Mr. Kay will now re-examine you. Mr. Kay, you may proceed.
