utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And then finally, if we go to Prosecution Exhibit 1223, a document dated the 11th of October, 1995, from the Knin Garrison, sent to the lady who triggered the matter from the International Committee of the Red Cross, Carmen Burger. And we see references there. If we go to the bottom of the page, we see the name S. Borovic. On the 9th of September, the perpetrators were discovered and remanded to the investigating magistrate in Zadar. And in the next page there is further information on an unrelated case which is part of another inquiry, and we see that General Cermak signed that document. Again, is it correct that you've not seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. But it -- it completes the documentary chain. In relation to looking at that matter raised with you, is your opinion changed in any way or your -- what you know, whether Mr. Cermak was involved with having authority over the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said already, on a few occasions General Cermak did not have such authority. He received an inquiry by the ICRC. In order to comprehensively and appropriately respond to the ICRC's representative he had to be informed, and this he could only be if he requested appropriate information from the Zadar-Knin police chief. He received the necessary information, and as a decent person he forwarded all the details in the letter you showed to me. He sent it to the head of the ICRC by way of a response. I don't think there is anything in dispute in the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour, in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Any need for further cross-examination, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Me neither, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. De Landri. MS. DE LANDRI: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I may have a few questions for you. In your statement, paragraph 6, and I read it to you, it is about on the 5th of August, when you entered Vrlika, you said: "Nobody was killed in Vrlika, and no houses or stables were burned down." Now, we also looked at D606, and perhaps we could have that on the screen. In which it is reported, and I think the date of that document is the 8th of August, but we'll have an opportunity to look at it in a second, in which it is reported that six human bodies have been buried. Could you give us additional information about these bodies being buried? And perhaps we have to go to page --

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly cannot supply any information in that regard. There is a possibility that during the combat, as the territory was being liberated, those people were killed and then decently buried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you can't give us any specific information, and therefore your statement that no one was killed in Vrlika seems, well, to be less certain as you put it in your statement.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that no one was killed and that nothing was burnt down, I meant as of the moment that the military operation ceased, not during the military operation. There were murders in certain areas even following the end of combat activity. That is why I specified that there were no killings or burnings in my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the identity of the persons that were buried and circumstances under which they died, you cannot give any further details?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this moment, because as I am saying the area under my authority was too large, and I did really did not have the time to get everywhere. I had seven chiefs of different sectors subordinated to me, and 15 commanders of police stations that performed their duties. My chief of the police sector, Mr. Jure Radalj, and the then commander of the police station in Sinj, Mr. Bilobrk would probably know much more about that because they covered that area and their office was in Vrlika.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In this report on terrain clearance in the area of Vrlika municipality, it is also stated that 60 conscripts took part in it. Could you tell me, were these military conscripts? Were these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid I did not understand your question. What terrain clearance do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you look at the document, as regards terrain clearance in the area of Vrlika municipality until today, the 8th of August, and that was the date I had on my mind, although the document is dated the 9th of August, "please be informed that the terrain clearance unit, 60 conscripts, has accomplished the most important tasks, including." Now, you are reporting -- yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will try to help. I think it's a matter of translation in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Because the original says something different than the English text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is it the word after 60?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, it is the word immediately in Croatian text, the second word in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Second word --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: "Asanacija."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Asanacija."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe there is a problem in translation of that word because that word was translated as terrain clearance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So could be a misunderstanding between your questions and the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I would just read, and my pronunciation may be very bad, [Interpretation] "Regarding the sanitation and hygiene measures on the ground." [In English] Yes. That is now corrected on the record. These 60 conscripts the document is referring to, you are reporting, were they instructed by you?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, within the framework of the police administration, in addition to the police officers we also had fire -- fire-fighting service and a so-called civilian protection. The civilian protection at certain moments, whenever necessary, members of the civilian protection would be called to carry out certain duties. One of such occasions was Operation Storm and its aftermath. I sent members of the civilian protection, the 60 members of the civilian protection to carry out the sanitation and hygiene measures on the ground. The highest priority was to inspect the area to see whether there were any dead bodies. That was the highest priority. Graves had to be marked if there were any, plastic bags were used for the bodies for further proceedings and identification. Those were my men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Those were your men. That means that apart from the police officers that were in your teams, you also had, in addition to that --

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian protection and firefighters. I sent some members of the civilian protection and some of the firefighters to Knin to Mr. Romanic. On the 5th in the afternoon I sent a fire truck with drinking water for my men and for others as well because they had run out of drinking water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was mainly interested in better understanding where these 60 conscripts came from, and I do understand that these were persons under an obligation to perform the service as civil protection personnel, and they were under your command for the performance --

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian protection, they were engaged in natural disaster situations and such like, and then I would take a list and I would issue an order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, one final matter I'd like -- briefly like to put to you. You described how collection centres, I think you called them, were established. You made reference to the school and that -- yes. You said that: "Upon returning to Knin, I ordered the reception centre for old people and children to be established in the elementary school hall," and you said, "A few hundred people that had stayed in their houses remained, and my policemen brought them to the school and that the school was -- in two days was full of old people."

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I be allowed to explain, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd first like to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I'd like to know is if there were -- there were no men in these collection centres, able-bodied men, well, let's say between 18 and 60?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I could see, when I visited the collection centre, and I had a good look when I was searching for the in-laws of my friend Mr. Svestan Zadric [phoen], who had remained in Knin, as I told you he called me from Zagreb and asked me to look for them. Then I went to the -- my officers. I took the list of all those who were there, and I found the gentleman and his wife. They were mostly elderly people, but let me tell you also this: When I arrived in Knin on the 5th, in the vicinity of the military command I observed a larger group of elderly people, women, men, and children, who looked scared to me, and that's why I said to my chief, Radalj, that "a collection centre should be established for such people who wanted to feel safe."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is in your statement and already you testified about that. My question simply was whether able-bodied men, who you do not mention, were in those collection centres, of in that collection centre in Knin or the other one you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I assume that all the young people were in the other one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In the other one. Other collection centre or other school? What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was the UNPROFOR barracks where other people from Knin found shelter. There were quite a few of them there, and I suppose that some younger people might have been there as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but there was no place where able-bodied men between 18 and 60 would be received in any centre?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, listen, apart from this centre in Knin, I also had a smaller-sized centre near Sinj, and I told my officers to try and shelter even younger people in Sinj, not to let them stay in Knin. Later on I was told that there were some younger ones who were obviously able-bodied and fit for service, and they were sheltered in that collection centre near Sinj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there any civilian police activities aiming at identifying possible suspects of armed rebellion; that is, Serbs who may have been involved in the army of the -- the RSK? Because you do not say anything about that. Do I have to understand that no such police activity took place or that it was not something you considered worth mentioning?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mention that for a very simple reason: Nobody ever asked me. During the occupation of that area within my police administration, we had a department which tried to collect as much information as possible about those people who were involved in the armed conflict. Likewise, the service for the protection of the constitutional order, the intelligence service that had been established with the Ministry of the Interior, also dealt with that issue, and for that reason, as far as I can remember, the Service for the Protection of the Constitutional Order, after the liberation, compiled a list of people who found shelter in the UNPROFOR barracks who might have been charged with the armed conflict and that list was accompanied with all the materials that they had collected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I've been advised by Mr. Misetic that there is a translation issue. So if I can turn the floor to him on that score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's the translation of the phrase at page 72, lines 13 to 14, and I believe you mention it again. It's being translated as "armed conflict," and I believe the witness is using the phrase you used in your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is "armed rebellion." Now where -- and this will really be my last question. I'm not interested in details. I am just trying to complete my picture of the activities. Where were these younger, able-bodied men who could be suspected as having taken part in the armed rebellion and who were not in the UNCRO premises, where were they interviewed or were they held at anyplace.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, as far as I know, in the liberated area very few or no people who had been involved in the armed rebellion could be found. Either they fled together with the army or if they stayed on they found shelter in the barracks that was under the protection of UNPROFOR. Negotiations were conducted with UNPROFOR for a long time for those people to be handed over, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In my question I specifically excluded those who were on the UNCRO premises. So if I do understand --

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no other premises of that nature, and the police never questioned those people. If that was possibly done subsequently, then it was done by either the Sibenik or the Zadar Police Administration Crime Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those answers. I think I have -- I have no further questions for you. Have the questions by the Bench triggered any need --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's three times no. Ms. De Landri. MS. DE LANDRI: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cipci, this then concludes your testimony in this Court. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for patiently answering all the questions that were put to you both by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you safe trip home again. Madam Usher, could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say one thing. I enjoyed the attention. I enjoyed the comfort of the hotel. However, the stay was really too long. I should have stayed nine -- two days. I've stayed nine. I repeat, I am getting on. I have my own rhythm. I am used to my own ways, so I have been bothered by such a long stay. Still, would I like to thank everybody who has helped me feel comfortable in The Hague, and I must say I have felt comfortable in your courtroom as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's good to hear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any other procedural matters we'd have to deal with at this very moment. I may have missed something, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is -- because we're coming up to the break -- --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- there is the outstanding issue of a witness that we applied to add to our list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: His statement's been distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's Witness 43 or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Surak [phoen] 46. I'm sorry, forgetting the number. IC46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I can inform you that either -- I have already signed this morning a written decision on the matter. I think I did, so it may already have been filed. But if not, then I would sign it within the next hour because there's agreement. And your request, which was not objected to by the Prosecution is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm much obliged to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then any other matter? If not, then I'd first like to apologise to interpreters, transcribers, and all those who are assisting us by going on for such a long time, but it saves us another session, because we'll adjourn, but we resume on Monday, the 26th of October, at 9.00 in the morning, in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
